analysis.one_liner: Mandates dozens of offshore oil and gas lease sales off the Atlantic, Pacific, Gulf, and Alaska coasts.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 253-170 on July 25, 2012, but the Senate never voted and the bill died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Interior Department to hold a set schedule of offshore oil and gas lease sales between 2012 and 2017, adding areas that the Obama administration's five-year plan left out — the Mid- and North Atlantic, the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas off Alaska, the North Aleutian Basin, and tracts off Southern California. It also narrows the required environmental review: the Interior Secretary would no longer have to study a no-leasing option before opening new areas to drilling [S3] [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would get legally mandated lease sales in new waters, including off the Atlantic coast and off Alaska, plus a faster, thinner environmental review. Supporters also argued more domestic production would create jobs and help consumers, though new leases take years to produce oil.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to conduct roughly 30 named lease sales on a fixed schedule from 2012 through 2017, including sales in the Mid-Atlantic, North Atlantic, Chukchi Sea, Beaufort Sea, North Aleutian Basin, and Eastern Gulf planning areas that were not all in the administration's final 2012-2017 program [S5].

Requires a Southern California lease sale (tracts in the Santa Maria and Santa Barbara/Ventura basins) by December 31, 2013, limited to development from infrastructure that already exists or from onshore drilling [S4] [S5].
Supporters framed the bill as replacing the administration's plan to promote offshore energy production, job creation, and domestic supply [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, commercial fisheries, and tourism economies would bear the risk of expanded drilling in waters that had been off-limits, especially the Atlantic. The public's environmental review would be thinner, since the bill forbids the Interior Secretary from even studying a no-leasing alternative for the new sales [S4] [S5].

drawbacks.text: Opening the Atlantic, Alaskan, and Pacific planning areas to drilling exposes coastal economies — fishing, tourism, beach communities — to spill risk from operations that would take years to yield meaningful supply [S3] [S4].

The bill waters down the National Environmental Policy Act: for the new lease sales, the Secretary is 'not required to identify nonleasing alternative courses of action' and need analyze only a preferred leasing option and one alternative [S4] [S5].

The bill overrides the administration's five-year leasing program, substituting a congressionally dictated sale schedule for the executive process set up under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act [S2] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate winners are oil companies that would gain mandated access to new federal waters and a faster environmental review. The claimed public benefits — more production, jobs, cheaper energy — are distant and modest, since newly leased areas take years to develop, while the costs (spill risk to coasts, weakened environmental analysis) are immediate and borne by coastal communities. The provisions keeping military zones off-limits and limiting the Southern California sale to existing infrastructure temper, but do not remove, the concerns.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill on a mostly party-line vote in July 2012, but the Senate placed it on its calendar and never took it up before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 [S7].

narrative.text: The House Natural Resources Committee, chaired by sponsor Doc Hastings, reported the bill on a 24-17 vote on July 18, 2012 [S7].

The House rejected Democratic motions and amendments, including amendments by Rep. Markey, and defeated a motion to recommit that would have barred leases to companies violating Iran and Syria sanctions, 179-240, with Republicans voting nearly unanimously no [S7] [S8].
The House passed the bill 253-170 on July 25, 2012: 228 of 240 Republicans voted yes, while 25 of 191 Democrats joined them [S9].
The Senate received the bill on July 26 and placed it on its calendar, but never voted on it; the Congress ended January 3, 2013 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a Senate vote, the administration's 2012-2017 leasing program stayed in place and no new Atlantic, Alaskan, or Pacific lease sales were mandated. Coastal communities, fishing and tourism interests, and drilling opponents were better off; oil and gas companies lost the chance at the added lease areas.

for.name: Doc Hastings
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and reported it out of committee on a 24-17 vote.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

against.name: Louise Slaughter
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to bar leases to companies violating Iran and Syria sanctions; the motion failed 179-240.

against.name: Ed Markey
against.what_they_did: Offered amendments on the floor that were rejected.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split mostly by party — 228 of 240 Republicans yes versus 25 of 191 Democrats yes — and the motion to recommit was almost purely party-line: all 179 yes votes were Democrats and all 239 Republicans voted no [S8] [S9].

industries.note: The bill hands companies mandated lease sales in new federal waters — the Atlantic, the Chukchi and Beaufort Seas, the North Aleutian Basin, and Southern California — and strips the requirement that officials study a no-leasing option first. The added spill risk and weakened review fall on coastal communities rather than on the industry.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling services and equipment suppliers
industries.note: More mandated lease sales mean more exploration, rig, and platform work over the following years, with profits flowing to the drilling supply chain.
New drilling off the Atlantic and Alaska coasts puts fishing grounds and beach-dependent economies at risk of spills, the same waters the administration's plan had left out.
